The arrangement traded territory and cash for time.

Variants.Content: The Treaty of Jaén, sealed in 1246 after Fernando III of Castile took the city, made Muhammad I of Granada a tributary vassal of the Castilian crown. Granada surrendered Jaén and agreed to pay an annual tribute of 150,000 gold maravedís, known as parias. In return the Nasrid emir kept his throne and his lands beneath the Sierra Nevada. The arrangement traded territory and cash for time. Castile gained revenue and a secure southern frontier, while Granada gained the years it needed to fortify its remaining cities, and the Nasrid court went on to build the Alhambra on the Sabika hill above the city.

Castilian kings spent Granadan gold on cathedral building and royal campaigns, and the tribute paid for much of the crown's southern ambitions. Nasrid ministers knew that the parias was the price of survival. Each year's payment bought another season in which Granada could repair its walls and feed its garrisons without facing an invasion.

Armed escorts carrying bullion chests across the frontier grip their lances in tense silence. Gold buys uneasy truces, but the jinetes on the Granadan side and the Castilian caballeros on the other know a truce hangs by a frayed silk thread. Keep your girth tight, never drink from a stranger's skin, and watch the ridgeline for riders coming in from the mountains.

Silk spinners and olive tenders in the Vega surrender coin to tax collectors so the King can fill the Castilian gold carts. Under the 1246 Treaty of Jaen, our Nasrid lord accepted Ferdinand III's overlordship for a twenty-year truce, and the tribute that followed drains our purses. Still, our homes remain unburnt and our children sleep in peace.
